title: Remark 1.2 (Open Problem on Sparse Densities)
statement_text: The problem of finding the asymptotic rate of moderate deviations of subgraph counts in $G(n,m)$ (i.e. the asymptotics of $\log\mathbb{P}(D_H(G_{n,t})>\alpha_n n^{v-3/2})$) across the whole range of sparse densities $t=t(n)\to 0$ remains open.
context_text: For graphs $H,G$, $N_H(G)$ is the number of embeddings of $H$ in $G$, i.e. injective maps $\phi:V(H)\to V(G)$ sending edges to edges. Let $H$ be a fixed graph with $v$ vertices and $e$ edges, $N=\binom{n}{2}$, and $L_H(m)=(n)_v(m)_e/(N)_e$ the expected number of embeddings of $H$ in $G(n,m)$ (falling factorials). For $t=t(n)\in(0,1)$, $G_{n,t}$ denotes $G(n,m)$ with $m=\lfloor tN\rfloor$, and $D_H(G_{n,t})=N_H(G_{n,t})-L_H(m)$ is the deviation of the $H$-count; moderate deviations are deviations $\alpha_n n^{v-3/2}$ with $\alpha_n\to\infty$ (the standard deviation in the dense case is of order $n^{v-3/2}$). Writing $\binom{H}{P_2}$ and $\binom{H}{K_3}$ for the numbers of paths of length two and of triangles in $H$, let $\gamma_H(t)=\big(4\binom{H}{P_2}^2t^{2e-2}(1-t)^2+12\binom{H}{K_3}^2t^{2e-3}(1-t)^3\big)^{-1}$. The authors prove that, for $t$ bounded away from $1$ and $\binom{H}{P_2}\ge1$, $\mathbb{P}(D_H(G_{n,t})>\alpha_n n^{v-3/2})=\exp(-\gamma_H(t)\alpha_n^2(1+o(1)))$ (and likewise for the lower tail) when either $t\in(0,1)$ is constant and $1\ll\alpha_n\ll n^{1/2}$, or $\max\{t^{1/2}n^{-1/2}\log n,\,t^{e-3/2}\}\ll\alpha_n\ll\min\{t^{2e-5/2}n^{1/2},\,t^{e+2}n^{1/2}\}$. They first proved the results in the dense case ($t$ constant) and have only partially extended them to sparser regimes; the remaining sparse ranges are left open. This is a problem on random graphs (probability) rather than structural graph theory.
notes: Stated in Remark 1.2 as an open problem in prose form, without a dedicated labeled theorem environment. PDF source — math notation in surrounding theorems may be partially garbled.
paper_title: Moderate deviations of subgraph counts in the Erdős-Rényi random graphs $G(n,m)$ and $G(n,p)$
